iOS net Surface × sa_std Gap Census

This page is one volume of the cross-language std census batch (same batch: Rust full std, Go net, Python net, Java net, .NET net, Android net). iOS's “net std” has three layers: the low-level Network.framework (a parameterized model of connections/listeners/protocol stacks), the upper-level Foundation URLSession family (a session/task/delegate model), and, beneath both, the POSIX/BSD layer. There is also a layer of platform connectivity model that desktop std does not have (paths, costs, policy enforcement), which contrasts directly with the platform model on the Android page: the portable protocol/tool surface is compared against sa_std in four categories, and the platform model is registered separately.

First, the source reality: Network.framework and CFNetwork have no complete open-source release. All iOS-side data on this page is annotated by reliability grade (open source / open-source counterpart / official documentation surface); surfaces that cannot be obtained are registered as unverifiable, and APIs are never filled in from impressions — this page's coverage boundaries need to be read first, more than on other platform pages.

Method and Inventory Scale

Two-side mechanical extraction (scripts and artifacts in tools/ios_net_census/, re-runnable): the iOS side has three routes — the DocC crawler takes each page's symbol title/kind/introduction version; corelibs uses a Swift public declaration scanner (explicit public/open modifier determination, including members inside public extensions); Apple open-source headers use a C prototype extractor. The SA side parses @extern from .sai and #def from .sal. The iOS-side inventory totals 2,241 rows (Network documentation surface 1,711 + corelibs 454 + open-source POSIX 76). Classification is done at the granularity of 35 capability domains (a per-symbol 1:1 comparison is meaningless for parameter getters/setters, as on the other pages of the batch), and the four categories use the same methodology as the rest of the batch: directly mappable / needs modeling / model mismatch / existing equivalent. Result: existing equivalent 10, directly mappable 8, needs modeling 11, model mismatch 6.

Classification summary: existing equivalent 10 / directly mappable 8 / needs modeling 11 / model mismatch 6 (35 domains in total). The reading is the same as the rest of the batch: equivalents are concentrated in the protocol execution layer (socket/TCP/UDP/QUIC/WebSocket/HTTP execution), and gaps are concentrated in the organization layer (parameter objects, configuration objects, delegates/callbacks, protocol plug-ins) and the tool surface (cookie, URL operations, mDNS, proxy, encrypted DNS configuration) — the former needs modeling, the latter is simply not done yet.

Platform-Specific Models (a Layer Desktop std Does Not Have)

The following four groups are iOS's platform connectivity model, contrasted item by item with the Android page's “network capability model / metering and multi-network binding / platform-enforced policy”: the two vendors gave isomorphic platform answers to the same batch of questions, while sa_std, as a portable std, does not carry them as a whole — classification as model mismatch is a conclusion, not a defect.

Path and Cost Model

NWPath is a connection's “path snapshot”: status (satisfied/unsatisfied/requiresConnection), the ordered interface list, isExpensive (cellular metering), isConstrained (Low Data Mode), supportsDNS/supportsIPv4/supportsIPv6, the gateway list; NWPathMonitor continuously pushes path changes via callbacks. This is the same model as Android's NetworkCapabilities + ConnectivityManager callbacks, in two implementations: applications do not pick network interfaces directly; they declare requirements, and the system gives the current path and keeps correcting it. sa_std's corresponding position is empty (0 route keyword hits) — the only portable part is the “interface inventory enumeration” information surface (already listed separately as directly mappable); path evaluation and callback dispatch themselves belong to platform services.

Parameter Policy Constraints

Connection policy is written in NWParameters and declared with the connection: prohibited interface types (prohibitedInterfaceTypes), requiresDNSEncryptedResolution, multipath service tiers (handover/interactive/aggregate), service class (nw_service_class); on the URLSession side the counterparts are allowsCellularAccess, waitsForConnectivity (suspend and wait when connectivity is unreachable instead of failing immediately), isDiscretionary (timed by the system). Android's counterparts are per-Network binding and Private DNS modes. This kind of “policy as parameters” has no corresponding layer in desktop std: it requires a runtime with a system behind it executing the policy; ported to sa_std it could only land as application-layer conventions, not a std surface.

ATS Transport Security Enforcement Policy

App Transport Security is not an API: it has no extractable symbol surface; its carrier is the application's Info.plist configuration (NSAppTransportSecurity: TLS and minimum versions enforced by default, plaintext allowed for declared exception domains), enforced by the system when URLSession/Network.framework loads. It is therefore not inside any symbol count on this page; its shape and conclusion are registered here: same kind as the Android page's “platform-enforced policy” (cleartext policy, network security configuration), a platform enforcement layer, model mismatch. The only portable part is the configuration items themselves, such as the minimum TLS version, already counted in the TLS row's configuration surface gap.

Local Network Permission and Background Takeover

Accessing the local network (Bonjour browsing/publishing, LAN connections) requires system authorization (the Local Network privacy permission); when unauthorized, browsing results are redacted — service discovery on iOS therefore has an extra platform permission surface (the N11 protocol surface is portable, the permission surface is not). Background transfer is taken over by a system daemon while the application is suspended/terminated, managing URLSession background sessions and replaying completion events after the application restarts (the U7 row) — like Android's platform-managed downloads, this is a “the system lives on behalf of the application” model; sa_std has no process lifecycle to attach to, and it is registered as a whole as model mismatch.

Priority Shortlist for Closing Gaps (Portable Surface Only)

  1. The Cookie surface (U3): cookie parsing/serialization (the Set-Cookie/Cookie headers, the full attribute set) + storage + automatic attachment by configuration. Pure functions plus simple state, overlapping item 4 of the AT list; a gap named in common by multiple platforms in this batch.
  2. The URI/URL operation surface (U9): URL construction/joining/relativization, query parsing and generation, percent encoding/decoding (sa_std currently has only the single sa_std_url_parse function). Same as item 2 of the AT list.
  3. The TLS configuration surface (N6): ALPN, explicit SNI control, cipher suite sets, certificate verification callbacks, minimum TLS version. sa_std's TLS body and JA3/JA4 fingerprint surface are already strong; what is missing is exactly this configuration layer. Same as item 3 of the AT list.
  4. DNS record-type queries + encrypted DNS client configuration (N13): a query result model by record type (A/AAAA/TXT/SRV) (item 1 of the AT list) and DoH/DoT endpoint configuration — the iOS side, in the shape of “per-connection resolver configuration”, proves the product position of this layer's need.
  5. mDNS / DNS-SD (N11): service browsing/publishing/TXT records. iOS's Bonjour and Android's NsdManager are two platform implementations of the same protocol surface; iOS's local network permission surface is not ported.
  6. The local interface information surface (N18): interface inventory enumeration (name/index/address family/addresses). Echoing the AT list's “local network information” item; iOS has no public routing table API (unverifiable), so this item takes interface enumeration only, without the routing table.
  7. The client proxy surface (N14): HTTP CONNECT / SOCKS5 proxy configuration and tunnel establishment. Across the five-platform census of this batch, the proxy keyword on the SA side is constantly 0 — a systematic blank.
  8. Two small protocol items (the N7 sub-gap, N10): QUIC datagram and explicit IP ECN reading/writing — both pure increments on existing protocol surfaces, with no model risk, suitable for opportunistic batch processing.

Coverage Boundaries

  • Source grade is evidence grade: all conclusions about Network.framework are built on the official documentation surface (grade=doc) — the documentation surface gives symbols' existence and signature shapes, but does not guarantee verbatim agreement with the SDK headers (overloads merged on the same page count as one row per page; the ObjC/Swift two sides are merged on the same DocC page, the inventory is mainly the Swift surface, distinguished by the lang column). If SDK headers are obtained in the future, this page's counts should be re-run against the headers.
  • Differences between corelibs and Darwin: the URLSession family is based on the corelibs open-source implementation (grade=oss-swift). Known difference directions: background sessions in corelibs have the configuration symbols present but the takeover semantics missing (Linux has no corresponding daemon); some Darwin-specific behaviors (such as parts of the cache/credential persistence details) are stubs or absent in corelibs. For such surfaces this page classifies only by corelibs' actual symbols, lists the takeover semantics separately as model mismatch in the U7 row, and does not fill in symbols corelibs does not have from Darwin documentation impressions.
  • CFNetwork unverifiable: CFNetwork's C API surface (CFHTTPMessage/CFHTTPStream etc.) has no open-source release and no systematic symbol set on the documentation surface; this line registers it as unverifiable and it appears in no count. Security.framework (the lower layer of certificates/trust evaluation) is likewise not expanded — the U5 row's “server trust” stops at the URLSession challenge surface; the SecTrust configuration surface beneath it is unverifiable.
  • The POSIX layer extracted only three headers: bsd/sys/socket.h, bsd/netinet/in.h and Libinfo's two netdb headers; other Darwin headers such as ifaddrs.h (getifaddrs) were not expanded — the N18 conclusion is based on Network.framework's interface surface, and POSIX-side interface enumeration (such as getifaddrs) is not counted, a known under-coverage.
  • Extractor approximations: the corelibs scanner is based on explicit public/open modifiers and members of public extensions; public members written without modifiers in ordinary extensions are missed; the DocC crawler takes the reference closure, and isolated symbols not referenced by any visited page are not included (this crawl visited 1,712 pages with 0 crawl errors, and the closure converged). Most of URLResourceValues' 92 declarations are file/iCloud attributes; the parts unrelated to networking count only toward the inventory scale and did not enter the classification table (the classification table takes only its URL-construction-related surface, in the U9 row).
  • Platform models do not enter the closing shortlist: the six platform model groups — paths/costs/multipath/ATS/takeover/permissions (including the 6 model mismatch rows in the classification tables) — register only shapes and contrasts, and are not counted as sa_std gaps — consistent with the methodology of the other pages in the batch.
